query: Consider the following context: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered promising candidate materials for next‐generation nuclear reactors due to their superior mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability at high temperatures. However, the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu, commonly used in cooling systems, poses challenges in forming composite structures. In that context, which method can be used for large‐scale reaction and stable microstructure, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) processing for mixed powders of refractory alloy components and Cu can enable a large‐scale, rapid in situ reaction that yields a stable, phase‐separated microstructure, thereby mitigating the deleterious effects of the positive heat of mixing between Cu and refractory elements.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous blend of mixed elemental powders comprising refractory high‐entropy alloy precursors and Cu particles.
generation.intervention: Processing the powder blend using LPBF with carefully controlled laser energy, scan speed, and environmental conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions during rapid melting and solidification under an inert atmosphere with minimal oxygen contamination.
generation.structural_mediator: Rapid solidification that promotes limited diffusion, leading to a controlled segregation of Cu from the refractory matrix and minimizing intermetallic formation.
generation.mechanism: The rapid heating and subsequent cooling inherent to LPBF reduce the time available for atomic diffusion despite the thermodynamic drive for mixing, thus enabling the formation of a microstructure in which Cu remains as a separate, stable phase, reducing the adverse effects of the positive heat of mixing.
generation.predicted_outcome: A composite structure with distinct, stable phases of refractory HEA and Cu, retaining high mechanical strength and thermal stability suitable for nuclear reactor applications.
generation.baseline: Conventional casting or slow cooling methods, which allow prolonged high-temperature exposure and diffusion, typically lead to unwanted intermetallic formation and poor microstructural stability due to strong mixing tendencies.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to work when LPBF processing is precisely controlled; however, scalability and reproducibility across different alloy compositions and processing setups remain to be fully validated.
generation.uncertainty: While LPBF is promising for rapid solidification, the exact phase distribution and interface properties must be optimized. Variability in powder homogeneity and laser parameters could affect the outcome, necessitating further detailed studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of composite samples: one using LPBF processing for the mixed powder of refractory alloy constituents and Cu, and a control set via conventional casting. Characterize both sets using scanning/transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and mechanical/thermal tests.
measurements: Phase distribution and interface quality by SEM/TEM
Thermal stability and oxidation resistance under high-temperature exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the LPBF-processed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in phase stability and mechanical/thermal properties compared to the conventionally cast samples, or if a homogeneous intermetallic phase forms contrary to the predicted stable phase separation, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations
